title: I Moved My Laravel Blog from GoDaddy to Cloudflare Pages: Cost, Speed, What Broke
html:
My GoDaddy renewal cart opened with a total of ₹12,021.84 for one year of shared hosting. For a content blog where readers simply come to read articles, paying ₹1,000 every month just to keep an Apache server running felt pointless. I moved the entire site to a static Next.js export hosted on Cloudflare Pages, dropping my hosting bill to exactly ₹0. Here is what happened, what broke along the way, and what I learned from the move.

Last updated: 10 Nov 2026. All renewal numbers, uptime stats, and traffic figures in this post come from my own GoDaddy invoices, Cloudflare dashboard, and Google Search Console data.

The Quick Summary: Before and After

Before jumping into the migration steps, here are the exact numbers side by side:

Metric Old: GoDaddy (Laravel) New: Cloudflare Pages (Next.js)
Monthly hosting cost ~₹1,001 / month ₹0 / month
Annual renewal price ₹12,021.84 (incl. 18% GST) ₹0
Architecture PHP 8 + Apache + MySQL Static HTML/CSS export on global edge CDN
SSL Certificate Manual renewal / renewal hassle Free automatic Cloudflare Universal SSL
Old Mobile PageSpeed 61 / 100 Fast global edge TTFB
Database downtime risk High (MySQL crashes, connection limits) Zero (no runtime database)

Why I Left GoDaddy

Like many developers in India, I started TrendsWheel on shared hosting because it seemed convenient at the start. It ran on Laravel with a MySQL database. For a while, it worked fine. But over time, two big problems made it impossible to stay:

  1. The renewal price trap: Shared hosting plans look cheap during promotional first years. But when the renewal email arrives, the discount vanishes. As shown in my order screenshot above, GoDaddy wanted ₹10,188.00 base price plus ₹1,833.84 in GST and fees, making it ₹12,021.84 for a standard 12-month renewal of Web Hosting Deluxe.
  2. Database and server overhead for read-only content: A tech blog does not need a live database server running 24/7. 99% of my traffic consists of people reading an article. Having PHP wake up, query a MySQL database for the article body, parse Blade templates, and assemble HTML on every request was slow and completely unnecessary.

When my hosting period neared expiration, I decided not to pay the ₹12k renewal and moved the site to Cloudflare Pages. (If you are planning a similar migration, read my step-by-step guide to leaving GoDaddy without losing data).

Why Cloudflare Pages + Next.js Static Export?

Cloudflare Pages lets you host static frontends for free with unlimited bandwidth and automatic SSL. When you configure Next.js with output: 'export', it builds every article into plain HTML files at build time.

When a visitor visits a post, Cloudflare serves the cached static HTML directly from the nearest edge server (in Mumbai, Delhi, or wherever they are located). There is no server boot time, no PHP execution, and no MySQL query bottleneck.

How I Migrated the Site Without Changing URLs

If you have an existing blog, the number one rule of migration is: never break your existing URLs or slugs. If you change your URL structure, you lose your backlinks and your search rankings vanish.

Here was my migration workflow:

  1. Exporting posts to JSON: I extracted all published posts, categories, and author details from the Laravel MySQL database into clean JSON files stored under content/posts/.
  2. Carrying over images with identical paths: Over 1,000 image files from Laravel's storage/app/public/ were copied directly into the Next.js public/storage/ directory. Because the relative file paths stayed identical, no image link in any existing article broke.
  3. Building routes with generateStaticParams: I set up Next.js dynamic routes using generateStaticParams() to generate all posts at build time, ensuring strict URL parity with the original Laravel routes.
  4. Preserving 301 redirects: I mapped 37 legacy redirects from the old database into a Cloudflare _redirects file in the public folder so older moved links continue redirecting cleanly.

What Broke (and How I Fixed It)

Moving from a full-stack PHP framework to a static export sounds simple on paper, but real migrations always hit snags. Here are the four issues that actually broke during my migration:

1. The AdSense React Strict Mode Crash

On the old Laravel site, Google AdSense ads were rendered as simple <ins class="adsbygoogle"></ins> tags with an inline push script. But in React / Next.js with Strict Mode enabled, components mount twice during local development.

This caused (window.adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}) to execute twice on the same ad container, flooding the console with errors:

TagError: All 'ins' elements in the DOM with class=adsbygoogle already have ads in them.

The Fix: I created a dedicated AdUnit.tsx component using a React useRef flag (const pushed = useRef(false)). The ref prevents the second push call from running, eliminating the error completely.

2. Contact and Newsletter Forms Stopped Working

The old Laravel site had a contact form and a newsletter subscription box that stored entries directly into MySQL tables. In a static export, there is no server-side PHP script or database connection to handle form POST requests.

The Fix: I replaced the database contact form with a clean, spam-protected direct email button. For blogs, you do not need a custom database table just to receive a few contact queries a month.

3. The Google Search Console Collapse

Because the GoDaddy hosting expired before the migration was finalized, the site was unreachable for a brief window. Googlebot encountered connection failures, and my indexed pages plummeted from ~130 down to just 2 indexed pages.

The Fix: I generated a static XML sitemap index containing clean sub-sitemaps (sitemap-posts.xml, sitemap-pages.xml, sitemap-categories.xml), verified that https://trendswheel.com/sitemap.xml returns HTTP 200, resubmitted it in Search Console, and began requesting indexing for priority posts in batches.

4. Third-Party Scripts Slowing Down Mobile Scores

A bare static HTML page loads in under 200 milliseconds. But once Google AdSense and Google Analytics scripts are injected, mobile performance scores can take a hit. Loading ads immediately at top-level slows down First Contentful Paint.

The Fix: I added an IntersectionObserver to the ad component so ads are only requested when a reader scrolls within 300px of their placement. This keeps initial page loads fast while preserving ad viewability.

Uptime Tracking: Starting the Clock

To verify that Cloudflare Pages is genuinely reliable compared to traditional shared hosting, I set up a free 5-minute HTTP/s monitor on UptimeRobot. The monitor tracks live availability 24 hours a day, and I will be publishing full 14-day uptime and latency logs in our upcoming hosting test post.

Who Should (and Shouldn't) Move to Static Hosting

You should make this move if:

  • You run a content-based blog, personal site, or documentation hub.
  • You are paying ₹5,000 to ₹15,000+ per year on cPanel or shared hosting renewals.
  • You want zero server maintenance, zero database crashes, and automatic global SSL.
  • You are comfortable editing posts in Markdown or JSON and pushing updates via Git.

You should stay on dynamic hosting (VPS or managed PHP) if:

  • You run an eCommerce store (WooCommerce, Magento) requiring dynamic checkout and cart state.
  • Your website requires user registration, login dashboards, or dynamic database queries on every click.
  • You rely heavily on non-technical team members who cannot work without a WordPress or Laravel admin dashboard.

The Verdict

Leaving GoDaddy for Cloudflare Pages saved me ₹12,021.84 every year. The site is faster, immune to database crashes, and hosted on one of the fastest global content delivery networks in the world for free.

The trade-off is that publishing now happens through a Git workflow rather than an admin dashboard. For a developer or serious blogger, that trade-off is well worth the savings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Cloudflare Pages really 100% free for blogs?

Yes. Cloudflare Pages free tier includes unlimited bandwidth, up to 500 builds per month, and free SSL on custom domains. For a content site, you will rarely exceed these limits.

Can I still run Google AdSense on Cloudflare Pages?

Yes. Google AdSense runs entirely in the visitor's browser. As long as your domain is approved and you add your ads.txt file to your public directory, AdSense units render normally on static pages.

What happens to my old Laravel database content?

Your content does not vanish. You export the post title, HTML, and metadata into JSON or Markdown files once. From then on, your content lives safely in your code repository.
